title: Candlemas (2 February)
hookLine: the Presentation: candles blessed for the year, a light to the Gentiles

cards: February 2 is Groundhog Day in America: a furry weather forecaster in Pennsylvania, a crowd in the cold, six more weeks of winter or an early spring. The date has an older name.
In Europe it was Candlemas, the day people carried candles to church to be blessed, and an old country saying held that a sunny Candlemas meant more winter to come.
The usual story is that the groundhog inherited that weather lore. The church kept the candles. Forty days after Christmas, a light comes into the temple.

teach.b: Luke tells it. Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple in Jerusalem to do what the law of Moses asked: a firstborn son presented to the Lord, and an offering for the mother's purification.
They bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb. A poor family, quietly keeping the rules.

teach.h: SIMEON TAKES HIM IN HIS ARMS.
teach.b: Then a man named Simeon, who had been told he wouldn't die before seeing the Lord's anointed, takes the child in his arms and blesses God.
The Church still sings his words every night at Night Prayer, in Latin the Nunc dimittis, now dismiss.
He can go in peace, he says, for his eyes have seen salvation, and he calls the child, in the Douay-Rheims: "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel."
Light for the nations, and glory for Israel, both at once.

Then he warns Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul. And an aged widow named Anna, who never leaves the temple, speaks of the child to all who are waiting. Tradition ties the day's custom to that line about light.
The priest blesses candles, and the people walk into church with them lit, carrying the light the way Simeon carried the child.

teach.h: A LIGHT TO THE REVELATION OF THE GENTILES.
teach.b: Some families take blessed candles home to light through the year, during storms, sickness and at the bedside of the dying.
Since 1997 it has also been the World Day for Consecrated Life, for nuns, religious brothers and others vowed to God.

how: On February 2, the feast of the Presentation of the Lord, Catholic parishes bless candles and may begin Mass with a candlelit procession; some people take blessed candles home for use through the year.

games.q: you're Simeon. you've waited a long time, and now the child is in your arms. what do you say?
o: ask how long you have left.
say you can now go in peace, for you've seen salvation.
ask the parents to stay with you.
games.why: now thou dost dismiss thy servant in peace. he calls the child a light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

practice: Light a candle, a blessed one from church if you have it, and sit with the flame.
Think of Simeon, who waited and then held what he'd been waiting for, and let your own long wait sit there with the light, without demanding an answer.
If you pray, pray Simeon's words, now thou dost dismiss thy servant in peace; if not, let the flame keep you company.

wordCard.voice: Candlemas. The old name for the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, when candles are blessed and carried, forty days after Christmas. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: now you dismiss, the first words of Simeon's song in Luke 2:29.

carryVoice: Your line: a light to the nations. Simeon held it in his arms. Until tomorrow.
